Rotation is the planned alternation of crops over several seasons or years, often to prevent soil depletion and limit

diseases or pests specific to a plant family.

Succession is the sequence of crops grown in the same space over the course of a year or short cycles.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour LA ROTATION

pages.title: In our specific context, strict crop rotation is not essential because:
pages.text:
The soil is continuously improved (compost, permanent cover, organic inputs).

Weeds are limited by breaks and green manure crops.

Crop diversity naturally reduces risks.

What matters most is thoughtful succession and simple alternation between families, root types, and nutritional needs.

To make your crop choices easier and avoid risky crop rotations, you can use three main tools:

1. Crop combination tables

Indicate recommended and discouraged crop rotations.

Allow you to plan quickly based on the crop currently in place.

2. Plant fact sheets

Provide information on compost requirements, cycle length, and disease susceptibility.

Help you decide which crop to plant next based on the season, soil, and market.

3. Plant classification chart

Classifies crops by botanical family and root type.

Helps you avoid planting crops too close together or with root systems that compete for the same soil layers.

1. Monoculture

Growing the same plant several times in a row in the same space. This depletes the soil in a targeted manner and

promotes crop-specific diseases.

2. Alternating between plants of the same botanical family

Even if the plants are different, they often share the same pests and diseases.

3. Alternating between plants with the same type of root

The same type of root requires the same depth of soil and often has the same weaknesses when it comes to pests.

4. Alternating between two very demanding crops

Growing two nutrient-hungry crops in succession, without a break or green manure, severely depletes the soil. Both

require a lot of compost, water, and care.

Some crops partially escape the general rules of crop rotation. Here are two types of cases to be aware of:

1. Low-impact crops (tolerance to repetition): certain plants with very short cycles, low requirements, and low susceptibility

to disease can be grown twice in a row without significant risk, provided the soil remains fertile and healthy.

2. Buffer or transition crops: certain plants are considered neutral because they:

have few requirements,

are not very susceptible to disease,

do not belong to problematic families.

They can be used as a transition crop between two more demanding or risky crops.

pages.title: Another planning strategy is to plant one main crop per season. You choose a crop that is suited to the climate, then change to a
pages.text:
different crop the following season.

Advantages:

Adapted to local climatic conditions

Fewer diseases (thanks to the change of seasons)

Simplified planning

Even if some crop rotations do not follow the classic rules of alternation, the change of season is often enough to break disease

cycles. Consider incorporating green manure or straw mulch every 2–3 cycles.

pages.title: Green manure
pages.text:
Green manure comes from plants harvested for mulching, such as millet or sorghum. Along with rests periods, they are

essential for keeping soil alive and fertile. Green manure is useful for the following reasons:

It protects against erosion, structures the soil, and provides organic matter.

They break disease cycles.

They smother unwanted weeds and inhibit weed seed germination, especially when the compost added is not fully

mature.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Engrais verts

pages.title: Rest period
pages.text:
Regarding active rest:

Mulching without cultivation for 1 to 2 months.

Allows the soil to regenerate and breaks disease cycles.

Adds organic matter with mulching.

Plastic mulching (with a tarpaulin, for example) can be used to accelerate composting, maintain soil moisture, and

prevent unwanted plants.

A black tarpaulin warms the soil, while a white tarpaulin maintains the temperature.
pages.illustration_description: Illustration pédagogique pour Période de repos

pages.title: Green manure

When should they be incorporated?

Between two demanding crops,

During difficult seasons (heavy rain or high temperatures),

After 2 or 3 successive crops.

Good crop rotation is based on three simple principles:

1. Change botanical families

2. Vary root types

3. Balance soil requirements

Adapt your strategy to the season, crop duration, and soil condition. Where possible, consider incorporating breaks with

green manure or straw mulch to naturally regenerate the soil.
